lines: {target}? Dry cliffs make every mistake echo.
No one should approach Badlands without hearing this. Carry water and watch the ledges.
Red sand and terracotta do not soften a fall.
I'll remember Badlands as hard country with old color in its bones.
Some danger announces itself. What stayed hidden at the badlands?
Where would you leave a marker if you had to approach the badlands again?
Did your boots hold when dust, loose stone, and hard clay became dangerous?
What did you cover first when the weather turned near the badlands?
Did every mouthful you carried last as long as you needed it to?
At least a river tells you which way it is moving. Did the badlands tell you anything?
Did worry take your appetite before the supplies ran low?
Was your pack too heavy when the ground became difficult?
Did anyone sleep well while heat hiding how tired you were remained close?
Did anyone keep their nerve when the rest of you were tired?
Does the smell of the badlands linger more than the rest of the memory?
Did the danger find you before you found a safe route?
Did anyone speak much on the way back, or were you all spent?
If the village wrote one warning about the badlands, what should it say?
Did you feel safe only after the village door closed behind you?
What unfinished question could ever pull you back toward the badlands?
{target}? Heat makes thirst louder than judgment.
If someone goes to Desert, tell them this. Carry water and travel by shade when you can.
Sand hides holes, husks, and bad footing.
I'll remember Desert as dry land that asks too much of the mouth.
When the danger first showed itself near the desert, did you have room to back away?
If I followed your route to the desert, where would I be most likely to lose it?
Good footing is easy to miss until it disappears. Where did yours disappear?
I trust a route less when the sky changes. What was it like over the desert?
Did the lack of water become its own danger near the desert?
I know how to read a current. I am not sure I could read the desert.
Plain bread can feel like a feast after a place like the desert.
Show me the gear that took the worst of the desert. I want to see the marks.
Did shade that lasted through midday hold until daylight?
Did the group argue before the danger or only after it passed?
Which sound from the desert still follows you into quiet rooms?
Could you avoid a fight, or had the danger already closed the way?
Did the route home before the light failed feel harder once everyone was tired?
Did the journey change how you prepare for ordinary roads?
I know the look of someone remembering bad water. A trip to the desert can leave something similar.
If you went back, what would you pack before anything else?
{target}? Wind has carved the land into bad footing.
Anyone bound for Eroded Badlands should hear this. Stay off narrow spires unless you can fly.
Red towers look sturdy until the path narrows.
I'll remember Eroded Badlands as badlands worn sharp by weather.
Once heat hiding how tired you were became a problem, could you still turn around?
Which landmark helped you remember the route home before the light failed?
Where around the eroded badlands did one careful step matter most?
Weather has ruined kinder roads than that. How did your supplies hold up?
A fisherman thinks about water even on dry ground. What water could you count on there?
My worst crossing sounds manageable beside what happened at the eroded badlands.
What did you eat when the road near the eroded badlands ran longer than planned?
How well did water, a head covering, and sound boots survive the trip to the eroded badlands?
When you finally stopped near the eroded badlands, what did you put between yourself and danger?
Would you trust the same people beside you at the eroded badlands again?
What sound meant safety was finally close?
What kept the first bad encounter from becoming the last one?
What did you promise yourself while the route home before the light failed stretched ahead?
What warning would you give before anyone else heads toward the eroded badlands?
You do not have to make the eroded badlands sound braver than it felt.
Does curiosity still point toward the eroded badlands, or has good sense won?
{target}? Dry grass takes warning from the wind.
Before another traveler leaves for Savanna, warn them. Mind fire and travel while the sun is kind.
Acacia trees lean like they heard bad news.
I'll remember Savanna as warm grassland where the wind talks first.
Was the worst part of the savanna obvious, or did it wait until you were committed?
How much of the journey to the savanna depended on landmarks instead of a map?
How badly did dust, loose stone, and hard clay slow you down?
Which came first near the savanna, the bad weather or the bad decision?
Did you carry enough clean water to cook near the savanna?
A boat has edges you can understand, while a trip to the savanna sounds less honest.
Was any food still dry when you finally stopped?
What broke first near the savanna, and how did you manage without it?
A dry bed changes the memory of a hard road. Did you find one?
If you returned to the savanna, whom would you ask to come along?
I judge weather by sound on the water. What sound guided you near the savanna?
Did putting distance behind you make the danger any easier to judge?
Did you save enough strength for the road home?
Someone will hear this and go anyway. What must they remember?
You look farther away when you speak about the savanna. Does it still feel close?
Could better weather ever persuade you to take that road again?
{target}? High dry ground lets trouble see far.
Pass this along to whoever visits Savanna Plateau. Watch cliffs and keep water close.
Acacia shade is thin comfort.
I will remember Savanna Plateau as dry high land with a long view of danger.
What made you lower your voice when you reached the savanna plateau?
Did you mark the turns near the savanna plateau, or trust yourself to remember them?
I know what wet docks do to balance. What did dust, loose stone, and hard clay do to yours?
What did heat by day and cold after dark do to your plans?
What would you have traded for a clean drink near the savanna plateau?
A leaking boat can be patched. I would not know where to start with the savanna plateau.
I hope somebody saved supper for the return from the savanna plateau.
How much of your gear came back needing repair?
Could anyone sleep near the savanna plateau, or did you keep watch until morning?
Did you have someone watching the way back while you watched ahead?
Tell me what the place sounded like at night. That usually reveals the truth.
At the savanna plateau, which threat made everyone change plans fastest?
Which familiar landmark finally let you breathe normally again?
What did the savanna plateau teach you that a map never could?
Did returning home settle the fear, or merely give it somewhere quiet to sit?
Would you return to the savanna plateau if someone you trusted asked?
{target}? Dry grass and hard wind share the same warning.
The next person heading toward Windswept Savanna needs your warning. Mind fire, cliffs, and the road back.
Acacia trees look like they are leaning away from trouble. I will remember that when I coil the rope.
I will remember Windswept Savanna as savanna country pulled sharp by wind.
Before things went wrong at the windswept savanna, what warning did everyone miss?
The path back matters more than the path in. What did you use to find it?
What sort of footing gave you the most trouble near the windswept savanna?
Could you see the way home once wind changing across the ridge began?
What did you rely on for drinking water near the windswept savanna?
The dock will feel wonderfully ordinary after hearing that story.
What food would you carry twice as much of if you returned?
I would check every knot after that journey. What needs mending now?
Which place did you choose for camp, and what made you trust it?
Tell me you had steady company on that road.
Did the sounds around you make the danger seem closer than it was?
How much luck was left by the time you got clear?
How long did it take before the village felt close again?
What do people misunderstand most when they talk about the windswept savanna?
Some journeys stay in the hands after the road ends. Is this one of them?
Would you guide another traveler there, or only warn them away?
{target}? Trees on badlands still grow in hard country.
Make sure travelers know this before visiting Wooded Badlands. Watch the drops between trunks.
Wood and red stone make strange neighbors.
I will remember Wooded Badlands as badlands with enough trees to hide the edge.
At the wooded badlands, which risk looked small until you were standing beside it?
A tired traveler can mistake any path for home. How did you avoid that near the wooded badlands?
Did anyone fall when dust, loose stone, and hard clay turned worse?
How long could you travel once heat by day and cold after dark set in?
I hope you filled every bottle before the wooded badlands. Did you?
That trip makes a day in my little boat sound gentle.
Did you pack enough to share, or only enough to survive the trip?
Did wet, heat, or grit damage anything you depended on?
I hope your shelter had one good wall and no surprises.
Which traveler surprised you by staying calm near the wooded badlands?
Could you smell the wooded badlands before it came into view?
What looked harmless near the wooded badlands until it began moving?
How many days passed before your legs forgave the journey?
Which mistake would you refuse to repeat near the wooded badlands?
You came back changed, though perhaps only you can name how.
Do you think the place would feel different on a second visit?
